raw_text: {"schema_version":"chat_response_v1","response_type":"answer","answer_text":"For a red blood cell whose membrane is water permeable but impermeable to the relevant solutes, the extracellular solution's tonicity sets the direction of net water movement. In an isotonic solution, the extracellular fluid has the same osmolarity as the cell, and there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell [ev_004] [ev_001]; the cell keeps its normal volume and shape [ev_003]. In a hypertonic solution, the surrounding fluid has greater solute concentration than the cell, so water rushes out of the cell into the surrounding fluid and the red blood cell shrivels [ev_004] [ev_005]. In a hypotonic solution, the surrounding fluid has lower solute concentration than the cell, so water rushes into the red blood cell and it swells and may lyse [ev_004] [ev_003]. Water moves by osmosis, which is the movement of water through a semipermeable membrane according to its concentration gradient [ev_006]. No, \"no net water movement\" in an isotonic solution does not mean that individual water molecules stop crossing the membrane: the source states that there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell, although water will still move in and out [ev_004].","short_answer":null,"citations":["ev_001","ev_003","ev_004","ev_005","ev_006"],"refusal_reason":null,"follow_up_questions":[],"confidence":0.8,"tutor_question":null,"learner_attempt_evaluation":null}
